newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ records largest ever c/a deficit in yr to March.
newsitem.headline: NZ records largest ever c/a deficit in yr to March.

text.p: New Zealand's NZ$4.47 billion current acount deficit in the year to March 31, 1997, was its largest ever, Statistics New Zealand said on Friday.
The next largest deficit was $4.05 billion, recorded in the March 1986 year.
The March 1997 quarter current account deficit was NZ$723 million.
"This was less than the December 1996 quarter, but the usual December to March seasonal impovement did not occur," SNZ said.
"After taking account of the seasonal influences, there was a sharp $695 million deterioration in New Zealand's current acount deficit between the December 1996 and March 1997 quarters."
SNZ said the main reason was a $532 million deterioration in the seasonally adjusted invisibles deficit.

All three invisibles components contributed to the deterioration: services, due to slower growth of inbound tourist numbers and their spending; investment income, due to a fall in New Zealand's returns from its overseas investments; and transfers, due to falling inflows of migrants funds and a fall in non-resident withholding tax collected.
"A $163 million fall in the March 1997 quarter seasonally adjusted merchandise trade surplus also contributed to the current account deterioration," SNZ said.
"The March merchandise trade deterioration follows an improving trade surplus in the second half of 1996."
Estimates of the trend in the current acount deficit have shown a deterioration since the June 1993 quarter.
"The March 1997 quarter trend estimates show a continuation of this long term decline," SNZ said.
"In the latest two quarters, this decline has been due to the worsening trend in the invisibles deficit, whereas the earlier decline was due to a falling trend in the merchandise surplus."
The current account deficit for the year ended March 1997 was 4.8 pecent of GDP. This compares with 3.7 percent for the March 1996 year, and 5.2 percent for the March 1987 year.
